bib.title: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Chapter 12: Continuous Latent Variables

read.skipped: nothing skipped; OCR text is noisy (figure labels and some pages garbled) but all 2249 lines were read, including exercises 12.1-12.29

question: How can data lying near a low-dimensional manifold be modelled with continuous latent variables, starting from PCA and extending to probabilistic, Bayesian, kernel and nonlinear versions?
contributions: Two equivalent derivations of PCA (maximum variance, minimum reconstruction error) and applications: compression, whitening, visualisation, N<D trick
Probabilistic PCA as a linear-Gaussian latent variable model with closed-form ML, EM, missing data and Bayesian/ARD dimensionality selection
Factor analysis as PPCA with diagonal noise covariance
Overview of ICA, autoassociative networks, mixtures of PPCA, principal curves, MDS, LLE, isomap, latent trait models, density networks, GTM, SOM

results.claim: PCA minimum-error formulation: the distortion J after keeping M components equals the sum of the discarded eigenvalues, so the principal subspace is the M largest eigenvalues.
results.setup: Any data set with covariance S; orthonormal basis, squared-distance distortion (eq 12.15-12.18), M<D
results.quote: which is simply the sum of the eigenvalues of those eigenvectors that are orthogonal to the principal subspace.

results.claim: When N<D, PCA via the N x N matrix X X^T has the same N-1 nonzero eigenvalues; D-N+1 eigenvalues of S are zero.
results.setup: N data points in D dimensions, N<D; centred N x D data matrix X (eqs 12.26-12.30)
results.quote: (which itself has an additional D - N + 1 eigenvalues of value zero)

results.claim: Eigenproblem cost drops from O(D^3) to O(N^3) with the N x N trick (printed as O(N3), O(D3)).
results.setup: N<D; cost of the eigendecomposition only
results.quote: Thus we can solve the eigenvector problem in spaces of lower dimensionality with computational cost O(N3 ) instead of O(D3 ).

results.claim: Evaluating C^-1 in probabilistic PCA costs O(M^3) instead of O(D^3) by inverting the M x M matrix M.
results.setup: PPCA, C = W W^T + sigma^2 I, matrix inversion identity (12.40)
results.quote: the cost of evaluating C- 1 is reduced from O(D3 ) to O(M3 ).

results.claim: In the ML solution of PPCA the noise variance sigma^2 is the average of the discarded eigenvalues; variance along retained axes is reproduced exactly (lambda_i).
results.quote: Thus the model predicts a noise variance orthogonal to the principal subspace, which, from (12.46), is just the average of the discarded eigenvalues.

results.claim: PPCA covariance has DM + 1 - M(M-1)/2 free parameters, linear in D for fixed M.
results.setup: Covariance C=WW^T+sigma^2 I, W is D x M, minus M(M-1)/2 rotation redundancy (eq 12.51)
results.quote: we see that R has a total of M(M -1)/2 independent parameters.
results.note: Eq 12.51 is printed DM + 1 - M(M - 1)/2; the lines before give DM+1 for W and sigma^2 and M(M -1)/2 for R

results.claim: A full-covariance Gaussian has D(D+1)/2 covariance parameters; PPCA with M=D-1 recovers it and M=0 gives the isotropic case.
results.quote: Recall that a general Gaussian distribution has D(D + 1)/2 independent parameters in its covariance matrix

results.claim: EM for PPCA avoids forming the covariance matrix: dominant cost is O(NDM) per sweep versus O(ND^2) to form S.
results.setup: Large D, M<<D; compares eigendecomposition O(D^3), O(MD^2) for top M, snapshot method O(N^3)
results.quote: the most computationally demanding steps are those involving sums over the data set that are 0 (NDM).
results.note: OCR prints the O of O(NDM) as a zero. Text also gives O(ND 2 ) for evaluating S and O(N3 ) for the snapshot method

results.claim: EM for PPCA can run on-line and handle values missing at random; the sigma^2 -> 0 limit gives a simple EM for standard PCA (E: Omega=(W^T W)^-1 W^T X^T, M: W=X^T Omega^T (Omega Omega^T)^-1).
results.setup: Roweis 1998 algorithm as described by Bishop, eqs 12.58-12.59
results.quote: Note that this EM algorithm can be implemented in an on-line form in which each D-dimensional data point is read in and processed and then discarded before the next data point is considered.

results.claim: Bayesian PCA with ARD prunes surplus latent dimensions: on 300 points in D=10 (sd 1.0 in 3 directions, 0.5 in 7) it suppresses 6 surplus columns of W, leaving 3.
results.setup: Synthetic Gaussian data, N=300, D=10, 3 high-variance directions; model M=D-1=9 implied; evidence-approximation re-estimation of alpha_i interleaved with EM; Fig 12.14
results.quote: The synthetic data sel comprises 300 data points in D = 10 dimensions sampled from a Gaussian distribution having standard deviation 1.0 in 3 directions and standard deviation 0.5 in the remaining 7 directions
results.note: Caption says 'the left-hand plot ... and the left-hand plot' (second should be right-hand). The M used is not stated in the caption; M=9 is inferred from 'suppressing the 6 surplus degrees of freedom' and the 3 true directions

results.claim: Gibbs sampling of Bayesian PCA hyperparameters shows three posterior modes, switching between them.
results.setup: Synthetic data, D=4, latent M=3, generated from PPCA with one high-variance direction; Fig 12.15
results.quote: This result shows clearly the presence of three distinct modes in the posterior distribution.

results.claim: PPCA fit with 30% of the variable values randomly omitted gives a visualization very similar to the complete-data one.
results.setup: Oil flow data, first 100 data points, PPCA 2-D latent projection, EM for missing values; Fig 12.11
results.note: Caption is OCR-garbled; 'first 100 data points' reconstructed from garbled text; the qualitative similarity is the authors' visual judgement, no metric

results.claim: Real data sets lie near low-dimensional manifolds: translated and rotated 64 x 64 digits in a 100 x 100 image have three degrees of freedom in a 10,000-dimensional space.
results.quote: The data points will therefore live on a subspace of the data space whose intrinsic dimensionality is three.

results.claim: Oil flow data: 12 measurements but only two degrees of freedom of variability (oil fraction, water fraction), so points lie near 2-D manifold segments.
results.source: Bishop and James (1993), via the book's Appendix A; not named in this chapter
results.setup: Oil flow data set, one geometrical configuration; Appendix A of the book
results.quote: there are only two degrees of freedom of variability corresponding to the fraction of oil in the pipe

results.claim: Kernel PCA works with the N x N Gram matrix, so it yields at most N nonzero eigenvalues even when the feature space has more than D (even infinite) dimensions, and cannot give a pre-image for the projection in general.
results.quote: Note, however, that the number of nonzero eigenvalues cannot exceed the number N of data points

results.claim: Autoassociative MLP with one hidden layer of M<D units, linear or sigmoidal, has its minimum-error solution at the PCA subspace; a four-layer network with nonlinear first and third hidden layers gives nonlinear PCA at the cost of nonconvex training.
results.quote: There is therefore no advantage in using two- layer neural networks to perform dimensionality reduction.

results.claim: PCA picks the maximum-variance direction and ignores labels, so it can overlap classes that the Fisher linear discriminant separates.
results.quote: PCA is unsupervised and depends only on the values X n whereas Fisher linear discriminant also uses class-label information.

results.claim: PCA whitening: y_n = L^-1/2 U^T (x_n - xbar) has zero mean and identity covariance.
results.quote: This operation is known as whitening or sphereing the data

results.claim: PPCA has a likelihood, so M can be chosen by validation log likelihood or Bayesian/ARD selection, and the model compares directly with other density models; the book notes a clean eigenvalue-spectrum gap is often not seen.
results.quote: The existence of a likelihood function allows direct comparison with other probabilistic density models.

limits: Chapter is a textbook treatment: few experiments, all illustrative (synthetic data, off-line digits, oil flow, Old Faithful); no benchmarks, error bars or comparisons against alternatives.
PCA and PPCA capture only linear structure and second-order statistics; zero correlation is not independence (Exercise 12.29), hence ICA.
Factor analysis has no closed-form ML solution and its latent coordinates are unidentifiable under rotation, which the author says made interpreting factors problematic.
Kernel PCA needs the eigenvectors of the N x N Gram matrix, so approximations are needed for large data sets, and a projection in feature space has no guaranteed pre-image in data space.

Nonlinear autoencoders need nonlinear optimisation with local minima and a pre-set M; SOM optimises no cost function and has no convergence guarantee; density networks need costly Monte Carlo marginalisation.
Bayesian PCA here uses an evidence/Laplace approximation valid for large N with a sharply peaked posterior, and puts priors only on W (mu and sigma^2 are point estimates).
Dated: 2006 coverage. Variational autoencoders, t-SNE, UMAP, randomised SVD and deep generative models are not covered; the chapter treats GTM/SOM/LLE/isomap as the nonlinear state of the art.
No hardware, runtime or compute numbers; complexity statements are big-O only.
practices: Centre the data and take the M eigenvectors of the sample covariance with the M largest eigenvalues; only M are needed, so use methods costing O(MD^2) (p.563).
When N<D, eigendecompose the N x N matrix X X^T and map back with u_i = (N lambda_i)^-1/2 X^T v_i (p.570).
Standardise variables measured in different units before PCA, or whiten (zero mean, identity covariance) when downstream algorithms need it (p.567-568).
For visualisation project onto the first two principal components (p.568); for classification-oriented reduction prefer Fisher's discriminant since PCA ignores labels (p.568).
Pick M from a gap in the eigenvalue spectrum if one exists, else use validation log likelihood under PPCA or Bayesian PCA with ARD (p.581-583).
For large D and small M use the EM algorithm for PCA (no covariance matrix, on-line capable, missing-at-random values) (p.578-579).
Use factor analysis rather than PPCA when per-variable noise differs; it is covariant under component-wise rescaling of the data (p.583-586).
Use ICA with a heavy-tailed latent prior such as 1/(pi cosh z) when sources are non-Gaussian; Gaussian latents cannot resolve rotations (p.591-592).
Do not expect a shallow nonlinear autoencoder to beat PCA; at least four layers are needed for nonlinear dimensionality reduction (p.593-595).
For nonlinear manifolds consider mixtures of PPCA, kernel PCA, isomap, LLE or GTM, noting the cost and local-minimum caveats given (p.594-599).

the eigenvector of the data covariance matrix with the largest eigenvalue
a separate linear rescaling of each variable to zero mean and unit variance
transforming data to zero mean and unit covariance using y_n = L^-1/2 U^T (x_n - xbar)
PCA as the ML solution of the linear-Gaussian model p(z)=N(0,I), p(x|z)=N(Wz+mu, sigma^2 I)
the columns of W in factor analysis, which capture correlations between observed variables
the diagonal elements of Psi in factor analysis, the independent noise variance of each variable
an independent Gaussian prior with precision alpha_i over each column of W, so surplus columns are driven to zero as alpha_i goes to infinity
PCA in a feature space phi(x), solved through the eigenvectors of the N x N centred Gram matrix K
a linear latent model whose latent distribution factorises, p(z)=prod p(z_j), with non-Gaussian factors
recovering unobserved sources and mixing coefficients from mixed observations alone
a network with the same number of outputs as inputs, trained to reproduce its inputs through a narrower hidden layer
a curve for which every point is the mean of all data points that project onto it, E[x|g_f(x)=lambda]=f(lambda)
a projection that preserves pairwise distances as closely as possible; equals PCA for Euclidean distances
a latent variable model with a regular grid of delta functions in a 2-D latent space and a nonlinear regression map, optimised by EM

problems: OCR of the scanned PDF is noisy: equation bodies are often lost, and many figure labels and some captions (Figs 12.2, 12.3, 12.5, 12.8, 12.11, 12.16) are garbled; page headers like 'Appendix A' appear as section headings.
Equation numbers (12.62, 12.63, 12.88) and several equations are missing from the text, so alpha_i = D/(w_i^T w_i) is not quoted.
Inconsistency in the chapter: Fig 12.14 caption says 'left-hand plot' twice (the second should be right-hand); Exercise 12.25 writes p(z)=N(x|0,I) with x for z.
Notation overlap: M is the latent dimension in Sec 12.1-12.2 but the feature-space dimension in Sec 12.3, where the retained count is called L (p.590).
The Sec 12.2.3 sentence naming the 'evidence approximation' is garbled in OCR, so the label 'Laplace approximation' used here comes from the next page (p.583).
Fig 12.5 image size (28 x 28, D=784) is partly garbled; 'D = 28 x 28 = 784' is inferred.
